title: Layering two commercial glazes for effect
subtitle: Applying a base glaze and a reactive top glaze to create colour break and texture
excerpt: Layering two commercial mid-fire glazes: a stable base and a reactive or textured top coat: produces colour effects that neither glaze achieves alone. Where the glazes meet and interact, you get colour breaks, depth, and surface movement. This tutorial covers the pairing principles, application order, thickness targets, and the test-tile process for predicting how a layer combination will behave in the kiln.
sourceNotes: Commercial glaze layering technique synthesised from studio ceramics glazing practice. Pairing principles derived from flux and colourant interaction behaviour documented in ceramics glaze chemistry reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: First-fired clay before glazing: porous and absorbent, which allows the glaze to adhere.
The visual transition zone where two glazes interact at their boundary, often producing a third colour or a variegated edge.
A standardised ceramic measure of heat-work in a firing: how much heat has been delivered over time.

content.text: Commercial glaze layering requires test tiles before use on finished work. Two glazes that are stable individually can produce runny, unpredictable results when layered. Always run a test tile for each new layer combination and examine the result before applying to finished pieces. Apply kiln wash to kiln shelves and keep a 15 mm clear foot ring on all pieces: layered glazes often run more than single-coat applications.
The principle behind glaze layering: the top glaze melts first (or at the same time as the base), and the fluxes in both glazes interact at the interface, producing a blended zone. The
colour break

appears where the top glaze thins out or runs away, revealing the base layer beneath. The visual richness of layered glazes comes from this variation: the thicker top-glaze areas look different from the thinner areas where the base reads through.
Choosing a layer pair

Effective layer pairs typically combine a stable, matte or semi-matte base (iron-bearing stonewares, celadons, or soft matts) with a more reactive or glossy top glaze that has a different colourant. Combinations to try at cone 6:
Iron-brown matte base + tenmoku (iron-black) top: produces rust-brown to black transition with iron breaks at the edges.
Celadon base + rutile or titanium top: produces streaky blue-green to cream transition.
White matte base + cobalt blue top: produces a crisp white-to-blue break at edges.
Running a test tile
Throw or press three small tiles from the same clay body as the intended piece.
Bisque
fire them at the same time as the main pieces. Vertical test tiles (leaning in the kiln, not flat) show running behaviour more accurately than horizontal tiles.

Apply the base glaze to each tile by dipping or brushing. Allow to dry completely. Apply the top glaze to the upper two-thirds of each tile only: leaving the bottom third as base glaze only, so you can compare base glaze alone and layered results from the same firing.

Vary the top coat thickness across the three tiles: one tile at standard application thickness; one tile with 50 percent thicker top coat; one tile with a thinner top coat. This shows the effect of thickness variation on colour break.
Fire the test tiles at the target
cone
. Examine: did the layered areas run? Is the colour break where you expected? Is there crawling?
Applying to finished pieces
Before applying to finished work, check that both glaze
specific gravities
match the test tiles. A change in specific gravity (through evaporation or settling) changes the application thickness and the visual result.
Dip the piece in the base glaze (or brush with a hake), allow to dry fully. Apply the top glaze by dipping, pouring, or brushing. Allow to dry fully before loading into the kiln.
Load pieces with at least 20 mm clearance from adjacent pieces in the kiln: layered glazes that run can bond pieces to each other if placed too close.

rows.problem: Glaze crawled into beads after firing
rows.cause: Base glaze not fully dry before top coat applied; too much shrinkage in the layered system
rows.fix: Ensure each coat is fully bone-dry before the next is applied. Thin both glazes slightly to reduce the dry-layer thickness.

rows.problem: Two glazes produced a uniform colour with no visible layering or break
rows.cause: Both glazes have very similar flux chemistry; top glaze dissolved fully into base during firing
rows.fix: Choose a top glaze with a significantly different colourant or surface character. Increase top coat thickness.

rows.problem: Layered section ran off the piece and fused to the kiln shelf
rows.cause: Top coat applied too thick; or combination more fluid than test tile predicted
rows.fix: Reduce top coat to a maximum of 60 percent of the thickness that caused running. Increase bare foot ring to 20 mm minimum.
